meta.subject: Anatomy
confidence_notes: The exact embryological mechanism of gastroschisis (used for comparison in this chapter) is still debated in the literature — theories include a vascular/ischemic insult to the developing abdominal wall (right umbilical vein or omphalomesenteric artery involution) versus a primary failure of body wall fold fusion; omphalocele's mechanism (failure of physiological midgut herniation to return) is more consistently described across sources.
meta.scope_note: An embryology/paediatric-surgery crossover topic with real clinical depth (mechanism, a major syndromic association with tumour-surveillance implications, and a frequently-tested comparison against gastroschisis) — scaled to 5 MCQs given its moderate (2-year) source occurrence and non-must-do status, while still covering the full breadth of what's actually testable.
meta.note: Representative, high-quality MCQ family for this topic, not necessarily exhaustive. Dedup pass completed against this file's own question set — no duplicates found. Includes a genuine image-based question.

core_knowledge.definition: Omphalocele (exomphalos) is a congenital anterior abdominal wall defect in which abdominal viscera herniate into the base of the umbilical cord, remaining covered by a translucent sac composed of peritoneum internally, Wharton's jelly in the middle, and amnion externally.
core_knowledge.classification: Classified by size (minor: <4-5cm defect, giant: larger, may contain liver) and by whether the sac is intact or ruptured.

structure_anatomy.embryological_basis: During weeks 6-10 of development, the midgut normally undergoes physiological herniation into the extraembryonic coelom within the umbilical cord (because the abdominal cavity is too small to contain the rapidly growing midgut at this stage), then returns to the abdominal cavity by about week 10-11 with 270-degree counterclockwise rotation. Omphalocele results from failure of the midgut to return to the abdominal cavity at the expected time — the herniated bowel (and sometimes liver) remains covered by the peritoneum/Wharton's jelly/amnion sac that would normally have been reabsorbed.
structure_anatomy.contents: Small and large bowel typically; in larger (giant) omphaloceles, the liver may also be contained within the sac.
structure_anatomy.cord_relationship: The umbilical cord inserts directly onto the apex of the sac — the defect is a true midline defect AT the umbilical ring, unlike gastroschisis.

clinical.associations: Strongly associated with other congenital anomalies (present in roughly half of cases) — chromosomal abnormalities (trisomy 13, 18, and 21), cardiac defects, and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (omphalocele + macroglossia + macrosomia + risk of hypoglycaemia from hyperinsulinism, plus increased Wilms tumour/hepatoblastoma risk).
clinical.diagnosis: Elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), confirmed by prenatal ultrasound showing a midline abdominal wall defect with a covering membrane and cord insertion at the apex of the defect.
clinical.management: Cesarean delivery is often considered for large or liver-containing omphaloceles to avoid sac rupture and to protect the liver from trauma during vaginal delivery, though this remains individualised. Postnatally, small defects may be closed primarily; larger ones require staged closure (e.g. with a silo) to avoid the abdominal compartment syndrome that immediate forced closure of a small abdominal cavity around too much viscera would cause.

concept_blueprint.related_structures: The key differentiating comparison in this topic is against gastroschisis — a different abdominal wall defect with a different embryological mechanism, no covering sac, a paraumbilical (typically right-sided) location, and a different, weaker association with chromosomal anomalies. This comparison is tested more often than omphalocele's own features in isolation.

question_family.coverage: The failure-of-return mechanism and the defining comparison against gastroschisis — the structural foundation for everything clinical.
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromic association, the AFP-to-ultrasound diagnostic pathway, and prenatal image recognition — the applied, clinically-testable side of the topic.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.concept: Failure of midgut return to the abdominal cavity
mcqs.question: Omphalocele results from failure of which normal embryological event?
options: Return of the physiologically herniated midgut to the abdominal cavity by around week 10-11
Closure of the neural tube by day 28
Fusion of the two lateral halves of the palate
Descent of the testis into the scrotum
mcqs.correct_answer: Return of the physiologically herniated midgut to the abdominal cavity by around week 10-11

distractor_rationale.Closure of the neural tube by day 28: An unrelated embryological event (its failure causes neural tube defects like spina bifida or anencephaly, not omphalocele).
distractor_rationale.Fusion of the two lateral halves of the: Relates to cleft palate, an entirely different developmental system.
distractor_rationale.Descent of the testis into the scrotum: Relates to cryptorchidism, unrelated to abdominal wall/midgut development.

explanation.core_concept: Omphalocele is best understood as an arrest of a completely NORMAL developmental step — physiological midgut herniation is expected in every embryo — rather than as an abnormal process happening from the start; the abnormality is specifically in the FAILURE OF RETURN, not in the herniation itself.
explanation.why_correct: Between weeks 6 and 10, the midgut normally herniates into the umbilical cord because the abdominal cavity is temporarily too small for the rapidly elongating midgut loop. By about week 10-11, the abdominal cavity has grown enough and the midgut normally returns, undergoing its characteristic 270-degree counterclockwise rotation as it does. Omphalocele occurs when this return fails to happen, leaving the bowel (and sometimes liver) persistently herniated into the base of the umbilical cord, covered by the peritoneum/Wharton's jelly/amnion that would otherwise have been resorbed.

why_others_wrong.Closure of the neural tube by day 28: A separate embryological system (neural tube) with no relationship to midgut herniation or abdominal wall development.
why_others_wrong.Fusion of the two lateral halves of the: Palatal development is unrelated to the abdominal wall/gut rotation process that produces omphalocele.
why_others_wrong.Descent of the testis into the scrotum: A genitourinary developmental process with no mechanistic connection to omphalocele.

high_yield_facts: Physiological midgut herniation is NORMAL between weeks 6-10 — every embryo does this.
Omphalocele = failure of the midgut to RETURN to the abdomen around week 10-11, not an abnormality of the herniation itself.
Because the sac represents persistence of the normal covering (peritoneum + Wharton's jelly + amnion), omphalocele always has a covering sac — a key differentiator from gastroschisis.
explanation.clinical_correlation: Understanding the timing (return expected by week 10-11) is why omphalocele can sometimes be difficult to definitively diagnose before 12 weeks on ultrasound — a small amount of bowel outside the abdomen before this gestational age may still be normal physiological herniation, not a true omphalocele.
common_confusions: Assuming the herniation itself is the abnormal event — the abnormality is specifically the FAILURE TO RETURN of an otherwise completely normal, universal developmental step.
related_concepts: Physiological umbilical herniation timing on ultrasound
exam_traps: Don't confuse 'failure of herniation' with 'failure of RETURN from herniation' — the herniation is supposed to happen; it's the return that fails in omphalocele.
other_ways_this_is_tested: This mechanism is the direct basis for the comparison question against gastroschisis elsewhere in this set.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: Omphalocele = failure of the NORMALLY-HERNIATED midgut to return to the abdominal cavity by week 10-11 — not an abnormal herniation event itself.
explanation.source_reference: Standard embryology — Langman's Medical Embryology, gastrointestinal system chapter.

mcqs.learning_objective: Explain omphalocele as a failure of the normal return of physiologically herniated midgut.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.question: A newborn is found to have bowel loops protruding through the abdominal wall, lateral to an intact, normally-inserted umbilical cord, with no covering membrane over the exposed bowel. Which condition does this describe, and how does it differ from omphalocele?
options: Gastroschisis — no covering sac, defect is typically paraumbilical (usually right-sided) with a normally-positioned umbilical cord, unlike omphalocele's midline defect with cord insertion at the sac apex and a covering membrane
Omphalocele — this is the typical presentation, with the umbilical cord simply displaced to one side
Gastroschisis — but it is otherwise identical to omphalocele in every anatomical respect
An umbilical hernia — a normal variant requiring no further evaluation
mcqs.correct_answer: Gastroschisis — no covering sac, defect is typically paraumbilical (usually right-sided) with a normally-positioned umbilical cord, unlike omphalocele's midline defect with cord insertion at the sac apex and a covering membrane

distractor_rationale.Omphalocele \u2014 this is the typical p: Omphalocele by definition has a covering sac with the cord inserting at the apex of that sac — an absent covering membrane and a separately-positioned, normal cord insertion are specifically NOT features of omphalocele.
distractor_rationale.Gastroschisis \u2014 but it is otherwise: Correctly identifies the condition but incorrectly claims no anatomical difference — the absence of a sac and the paraumbilical location ARE the defining anatomical differences from omphalocele.
distractor_rationale.An umbilical hernia \u2014 a normal vari: Umbilical hernia is a covered, reducible protrusion through a weak umbilical ring, typically presenting later in infancy, not exposed bowel loops at birth — a different condition entirely, and this presentation is not a benign normal variant.

explanation.core_concept: Gastroschisis and omphalocele are the two major congenital abdominal wall defects, and they are near-opposite in nearly every distinguishing feature — sac presence, location relative to the cord, and chromosomal association — which is exactly why they're almost always tested as a direct comparison rather than in isolation.
explanation.why_correct: The absence of a covering membrane over the exposed bowel, combined with a paraumbilical (typically right-sided) location and a normally-inserted, intact umbilical cord, is the classic description of gastroschisis — distinctly different from omphalocele, where a sac (peritoneum/Wharton's jelly/amnion) always covers the herniated contents and the cord inserts at the apex of that sac rather than being separately, normally positioned.

why_others_wrong.Omphalocele \u2014 this is the typical p: Misidentifies the condition — omphalocele always has both a covering sac AND cord insertion at the defect itself, neither of which is present in this vignette.
why_others_wrong.Gastroschisis \u2014 but it is otherwise: Correct on identification, but the claim of no anatomical difference contradicts the very features (sac, location, cord relationship) used to make the diagnosis in the first place.
why_others_wrong.An umbilical hernia \u2014 a normal vari: A fundamentally different, generally benign condition with intact skin/peritoneal covering and later presentation — doesn't match exposed, uncovered bowel at birth.

high_yield_facts: Omphalocele: COVERED (sac present), MIDLINE, cord inserts at the sac apex, STRONG chromosomal/syndromic association (~50% have other anomalies).

Gastroschisis: UNCOVERED (no sac), PARAUMBILICAL (usually right-sided), cord normally positioned/separate from the defect, WEAKER chromosomal association but higher risk of bowel complications (atresia, ischemia) from exposed bowel.
This omphalocele-vs-gastroschisis contrast is one of the most reliably repeated comparison questions in paediatric surgery/embryology.
explanation.clinical_correlation: The presence or absence of a covering sac has real prognostic and management implications: exposed bowel in gastroschisis is at risk of fluid loss, heat loss, and matting/ischemic injury from direct amniotic fluid exposure, requiring different immediate postnatal handling (bowel bag, careful positioning) from an intact omphalocele sac.
common_confusions: Trying to distinguish these two conditions using only 'is bowel outside the abdomen' as the discriminator — that's true of BOTH conditions; the sac, location, and cord relationship are what actually differentiate them.
exceptions: A ruptured omphalocele sac can superficially resemble gastroschisis at delivery (exposed bowel, no visible sac) — the umbilical cord's position (inserting at the defect vs separately positioned) remains a useful distinguishing clue even when the sac has already ruptured.
related_concepts: Elevated maternal AFP (seen in both, but more prominently associated with open defects like gastroschisis)
exam_traps: Don't use 'chromosomal anomaly present' as your primary discriminator without also checking the sac and cord findings — while omphalocele has the stronger chromosomal association in general, the anatomical findings described in a vignette are the more reliable and specific diagnostic clue.
explanation.memory_aid: Omphalocele = 'O' for cOvered, cOrd-at-the-defect. Gastroschisis = Gash in the wall, no covering, cord is Guiltless (normal, separate).
other_ways_this_is_tested: This comparison sets up the Beckwith-Wiedemann association question and the diagnostic/AFP question elsewhere in this set, both of which apply specifically to omphalocele rather than gastroschisis.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: Gastroschisis: no sac, paraumbilical/right-sided, normal cord position. Omphalocele: sac present, midline, cord inserts at the sac apex — near-opposite features, tested constantly as a pair.
explanation.source_reference: Standard paediatric surgery/embryology comparison — Langman's Medical Embryology; Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, abdominal wall defects section.

mcqs.learning_objective: Distinguish gastroschisis from omphalocele using sac presence, defect location, and umbilical cord relationship.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.question: A neonate with omphalocele is noted to also have macroglossia and marked macrosomia (large birth weight and length for gestational age), with an episode of hypoglycaemia on day 1 of life. Which associated syndrome should be suspected, and what tumour risk does it carry?
options: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome — increased risk of Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma
Down syndrome (trisomy 21) — increased risk of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) — no significant increased tumour risk
Prader-Willi syndrome — increased risk of pituitary adenoma
mcqs.correct_answer: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome — increased risk of Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma

distractor_rationale.Down syndrome (trisomy 21) \u2014 increa: Down syndrome can be associated with omphalocele and does carry increased leukaemia risk, but does not typically feature the specific triad of macroglossia, macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycaemia described here — that specific combination points more precisely to Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
distractor_rationale.Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) \u2014 no: Trisomy 18 is associated with omphalocele but presents with growth RESTRICTION (small for gestational age) and multiple structural anomalies, not macrosomia — the opposite growth pattern from what's described.
distractor_rationale.Prader-Willi syndrome \u2014 increased r: Prader-Willi syndrome is not classically associated with omphalocele, and its features (neonatal hypotonia, later childhood obesity) and tumour risk profile don't match this vignette.

explanation.core_concept: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is the single most important syndromic association to actively recall whenever omphalocele appears alongside overgrowth features, precisely because it carries a specific, actionable tumour surveillance requirement that changes how the child is followed after birth.
explanation.why_correct: The combination of omphalocele, macroglossia, and macrosomia is the classic triad of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, an overgrowth syndrome caused by dysregulation of imprinted genes on chromosome 11p15. Neonatal hypoglycaemia occurs from associated hyperinsulinism (pancreatic beta-cell hyperplasia). The syndrome carries a meaningfully increased risk of embryonal tumours, particularly Wilms tumour and hepatoblastoma, which is why affected children require structured tumour surveillance (periodic abdominal ultrasound and AFP monitoring) through early childhood.

why_others_wrong.Down syndrome (trisomy 21) \u2014 increa: A real omphalocele association and a real leukaemia risk, but the specific macroglossia + macrosomia + hypoglycaemia triad described here is not the classic Down syndrome presentation, which more typically features hypotonia and characteristic facial features without macrosomia.
why_others_wrong.Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) \u2014 no: Trisomy 18 causes growth RESTRICTION, the opposite of the macrosomia described, making this an anatomically inconsistent choice for this vignette regardless of the tumour-risk claim.
why_others_wrong.Prader-Willi syndrome \u2014 increased r: Not a recognised omphalocele association, and its clinical picture (neonatal hypotonia, later hyperphagia/obesity) doesn't match this presentation at all.

high_yield_facts: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome triad: omphalocele + macroglossia + macrosomia.
Neonatal hypoglycaemia from hyperinsulinism is a common, clinically important early complication requiring monitoring.
Tumour surveillance (Wilms tumour, hepatoblastoma) is a required, ongoing part of management for these children — not just a textbook fact but an actual clinical protocol.
explanation.clinical_correlation: Because of the tumour risk, children with confirmed or suspected Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome undergo scheduled surveillance abdominal ultrasounds (commonly every 3 months until around age 8) and serum AFP monitoring — recognising the syndrome at birth has direct, ongoing management consequences.
common_confusions: Treating every omphalocele-associated syndrome as carrying the same generic 'increased anomaly risk' without distinguishing WHICH syndrome carries a specific TUMOUR risk requiring active surveillance — Beckwith-Wiedemann is the one that specifically does.
exam_traps: Don't let 'omphalocele + any other anomaly' default to a chromosomal trisomy — the specific overgrowth pattern (macrosomia, macroglossia) should redirect you to Beckwith-Wiedemann, a distinct entity from the trisomies with its own tumour-risk implications.
explanation.memory_aid: Beckwith-Wiedemann = BIG baby, BIG tongue, BIG hole (omphalocele) — everything overgrown, including tumour risk.
other_ways_this_is_tested: This association question complements the comparison-with-gastroschisis question by reinforcing why omphalocele specifically (not gastroschisis) carries this strong syndromic-association teaching point.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: Omphalocele + macroglossia + macrosomia + neonatal hypoglycaemia = Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome — remember its distinct Wilms tumour/hepatoblastoma surveillance requirement.
explanation.source_reference: Standard paediatric genetics/oncology teaching — Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics, overgrowth syndromes and paediatric oncology chapters.

mcqs.learning_objective: Recognise Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome from its classic triad with omphalocele and know its associated tumour surveillance requirement.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.question: A pregnant woman has an elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) at 16 weeks' gestation. Which follow-up investigation is most appropriate to evaluate for a fetal abdominal wall defect as a possible cause?
options: Detailed fetal ultrasound
Maternal liver function tests
Amniocentesis for karyotype alone, without imaging
Repeat AFP testing only, with no imaging

distractor_rationale.Maternal liver function tests: AFP elevation in this context reflects a FETAL process (open defect allowing AFP leakage into amniotic fluid), not maternal liver pathology — maternal LFTs wouldn't clarify a fetal structural anomaly.
distractor_rationale.Amniocentesis for karyotype alone, witho: While karyotyping is often eventually relevant given the chromosomal associations of abdominal wall defects, jumping straight to an invasive test without first getting anatomical information from ultrasound skips the appropriate, lower-risk first step.
distractor_rationale.Repeat AFP testing only, with no imaging: A repeat lab value alone cannot identify or characterise a structural defect — imaging is required to actually see and describe the anomaly.

explanation.core_concept: Elevated maternal serum AFP is a screening clue, not a diagnosis — it raises suspicion for several possible fetal conditions (open neural tube defects, abdominal wall defects, and others) that all allow fetal serum proteins to leak into the amniotic fluid and maternal circulation, and detailed ultrasound is what turns that nonspecific clue into an actual structural diagnosis.
explanation.why_correct: Detailed fetal ultrasound is the appropriate next step to directly visualise the fetal abdominal wall, identify a defect if present, and characterise it (presence or absence of a covering sac, location relative to the umbilical cord, other associated findings) — distinguishing omphalocele from gastroschisis and screening for additional anomalies, all of which meaningfully guide further management and counselling.

why_others_wrong.Maternal liver function tests: AFP elevation here is a marker of a FETAL condition (leakage through an open defect), not maternal hepatic pathology — this test addresses the wrong physiological compartment.
why_others_wrong.Amniocentesis for karyotype alone, witho: Skips the essential anatomical characterisation step; ultrasound findings (e.g., presence of a sac) also help determine how urgently or specifically genetic counselling and testing should proceed, rather than ordering an invasive test blind.
why_others_wrong.Repeat AFP testing only, with no imaging: A repeated lab value provides no structural information and cannot by itself identify, localise, or characterise any anomaly.

high_yield_facts: Elevated maternal AFP + suspected abdominal wall defect → detailed ultrasound is the appropriate next step.

Ultrasound can distinguish omphalocele (sac present, midline, cord at apex) from gastroschisis (no sac, paraumbilical) prenatally, which has real implications for counselling about associated anomaly risk.
AFP is also classically elevated in open neural tube defects — a similar screening logic applies there, reinforcing why AFP is a general 'open fetal defect' marker, not specific to any one condition.
explanation.clinical_correlation: Once an abdominal wall defect is confirmed on ultrasound, further workup often includes fetal echocardiography (given the cardiac defect association) and consideration of genetic counselling/karyotyping — the ultrasound findings themselves help stratify how strongly to pursue these additional evaluations.
common_confusions: Treating an elevated AFP result as if it were already a diagnosis rather than a screening trigger that requires further, more specific investigation to interpret.
related_concepts: Open neural tube defects and AFP
Fetal echocardiography for associated cardiac anomalies
exam_traps: Don't pick an invasive genetic test as the FIRST step when a non-invasive imaging study can provide essential structural information first — sequencing of investigations matters in these questions.
other_ways_this_is_tested: This diagnostic pathway question complements the comparison and association questions elsewhere in this set by adding the prenatal detection angle to the postnatal/anatomical picture.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: Elevated maternal AFP suggesting a possible abdominal wall defect should be followed by detailed fetal ultrasound — the step that actually characterises the anomaly and guides further management.
explanation.source_reference: Standard prenatal screening and diagnostic pathway — Williams Obstetrics, prenatal diagnosis chapter.

mcqs.learning_objective: Identify detailed fetal ultrasound as the appropriate next step after elevated maternal AFP suggesting a fetal abdominal wall defect.

mcqs.subject: Anatomy
mcqs.question: [Image: prenatal ultrasound showing a midline anterior abdominal wall defect with herniated bowel contained within a membrane-covered sac, and the umbilical cord seen inserting directly at the apex of the sac.] This ultrasound appearance is most consistent with which diagnosis?
options: Omphalocele
Gastroschisis
Umbilical hernia diagnosed prenatally
Normal physiological gut herniation at 10 weeks

distractor_rationale.Gastroschisis: Gastroschisis specifically lacks a covering sac and has the umbilical cord inserting separately/normally, not at the apex of any membrane — the described findings are the opposite pattern.
distractor_rationale.Umbilical hernia diagnosed prenatally: Umbilical hernia is a postnatal diagnosis (a weakness at the umbilical ring becoming apparent after the cord has separated), not something characterised this way on a prenatal scan with cord-into-sac insertion.
distractor_rationale.Normal physiological gut herniation at 1: Physiological herniation is expected only up to about 10-11 weeks and is a transient, self-resolving finding — a persistent, clearly demarcated sac with contained bowel at a stage/context suggesting a structural diagnosis (rather than routine early gestational dating) points to a true omphalocele, not the normal transient process.

explanation.core_concept: The prenatal ultrasound diagnosis of omphalocele rests on the same anatomical triad used postnatally — a covering membrane, a defect at the umbilical ring, and cord insertion at the apex of the sac — visualised in utero rather than after delivery.
explanation.why_correct: A midline defect with herniated, sac-covered bowel and cord insertion at the sac's apex is the defining prenatal ultrasound appearance of omphalocele, directly mirroring the anatomical findings used to diagnose it after birth.

why_others_wrong.Gastroschisis: Would show free-floating bowel loops in the amniotic fluid WITHOUT any covering membrane, and a normally, separately positioned umbilical cord insertion — the presence of a sac with cord-at-apex insertion rules this out.
why_others_wrong.Umbilical hernia diagnosed prenatally: Not a recognised prenatal ultrasound diagnosis in this form — umbilical hernia is identified postnatally as a reducible bulge at the umbilicus after cord separation, an entirely different clinical scenario.
why_others_wrong.Normal physiological gut herniation at 1: This is a transient, expected finding only in a narrow early gestational window and is not diagnosed as a distinct 'condition' in the way omphalocele is — a persistent, well-defined sac finding presented as a diagnostic vignette points to true omphalocele, not this normal transient process.

high_yield_facts: Prenatal ultrasound omphalocele triad: covering sac + midline defect + cord inserting at the sac apex.
This should prompt further workup: detailed anomaly scan, fetal echocardiography, and consideration of genetic counselling/karyotyping given the strong syndromic/chromosomal associations.

Distinguishing this from gastroschisis prenatally (sac vs no sac, cord position) has real implications for counselling, since the anomaly-association risk profile differs meaningfully between the two.
explanation.clinical_correlation: Confirming omphalocele prenatally allows for coordinated delivery planning (considering caesarean delivery, especially for large or liver-containing defects) and immediate neonatal surgical team availability at birth — this image-based recognition has direct downstream clinical consequences.
common_confusions: Assuming any visible bowel outside the fetal abdomen on ultrasound before 11-12 weeks must be pathological — routine physiological herniation is a normal finding at this early stage and shouldn't be over-called as omphalocele without appropriate gestational-age context.
exceptions: Distinguishing true early omphalocele from normal physiological herniation before 11-12 weeks can be genuinely difficult on ultrasound — definitive diagnosis is often deferred until after this gestational window when physiological herniation should have resolved.
related_concepts: Karyotyping following an abnormal anomaly scan
exam_traps: Don't identify a sac-covered defect as gastroschisis just because 'abdominal wall defect' is the general category — the SAC and CORD POSITION are the specific discriminating details in this image-based format.
explanation.image_clues: Key findings: a membrane clearly covering the herniated contents, and the umbilical cord visibly inserting at the TOP (apex) of that covered sac, not separately from it.
other_ways_this_is_tested: This image-based recognition directly extends the postnatal comparison and diagnostic-pathway questions elsewhere in this set into the prenatal imaging context.
explanation.neet_pg_takeaway: Prenatal ultrasound: covering sac + cord inserting at the sac's apex = omphalocele — the same anatomical triad used postnatally, just visualised earlier.
explanation.source_reference: Standard prenatal diagnostic imaging teaching — Williams Obstetrics and standard fetal medicine/radiology references on abdominal wall defects.
